original_summary: Hanabi is a cooperative card game for 2 to 5 players. Each player holds a hand they cannot see but everyone else can. The team spends a limited supply of hint tokens to tell teammates about their cards, and tries to play five colour piles in order from 1 to 5 before three failed plays or the end of the deck.

review.evidence: Every simple policy fails. Always playing your oldest card burns the 3 fuses within a few turns, because only 15 of 50 cards are playable 1s at the start. Always discarding scores 0. Always hinting runs out of tokens and builds nothing. There is no seat edge, since everyone shares one outcome. Choices of what to hint, when to discard and when to risk a play decide the score.

Strong teams reliably score far higher than weak teams on the same deal. They spend hints efficiently, read the intent behind a hint, protect singleton 5s and avoid blind plays. The shuffle sets the ceiling of a deal, but most deals allow a high score with good play.
Perfect scores are rare even for experts, so there is always room to improve. A careful beginner who only plays fully hinted cards still scores a few points.

The core of the game is inference. You deduce your own hidden cards from hints, from the public discards and played piles, and from what a teammate's choice of hint implies about what they want you to do. That is opponent modelling in partner form, and it is planned over many turns.
The score is the sum of the pile tops. Every outcome follows from the card faces and the rules. No judgement is needed.

The game is turn-based and text-only. Problems: the 50-card, 5-colour deck makes games long (often more than 60 turns) and the state large. Hands hidden from their owner but visible to others are the inverse of the supported hidden hands. The result is a score, not a winner. The previous adaptation also overran the limits: it tracked a 15-cell copies table (23 or more numbers) and needed lookup updates that cost far more than 20 steps per turn.

problems: The full game (50 cards, 5 colours, hands of 4 to 5, up to 5 players) is too long and carries too much state for the 40-round, 20-attribute limits.
The original produces only a score, and the engine can only declare winners or a draw. A cooperative game needs a win threshold.
Owner-blind hands are the inverse of supported hidden hands, and the mechanism for showing each player the other hands was not stated.
The previous variation tracked a copies-outstanding table of 15 numbers. That pushed the tracked numbers to at least 23, over the limit of 20.
Updating a 15-cell colour-by-rank table on every play or discard needs lookup logic the engine lacks, costing roughly 15 to 20 steps by itself.
The copies table is redundant. It can be derived exactly from the public discard pile and pile values, so it spends budget without adding information.
The previous step count (12) was understated. Validation, hint resolution, the play test, the pile update, fuses, bonuses, the draw, the final round and the end checks were not all counted.
Hint matching done card by card, and the play test done as a 3-way colour lookup, would each cost several steps per turn.

changes.what: Use a 30-card deck in 3 colours (three 1s, two each of 2, 3 and 4, one 5 per colour), 2 to 4 players, hand size 5 with 2 players and 4 with 3 or 4 players, and a cap of 40 turns.
changes.why: This keeps the structure of Hanabi (scarce 5s, duplicated low cards, the hint economy) while making a game fit in 40 turns and a handful of tracked numbers.
changes.fixes: The full game (50 cards, 5 colours, hands of 4 to 5, up to 5 players) is too long and carries too much state for the 40-round, 20-attribute limits.

changes.what: Add a team target: the team wins if the final fireworks score is at least 10 (2 or 3 players) or 9 (4 players). Losing the last fuse sets the team score to 0. Every player's total equals the team score, and the engine's target rule declares everyone a winner or nobody.
changes.why: The engine can only declare winners. A threshold turns the cooperative score into a shared win or loss, and it needs real coordination to reach.
changes.fixes: The original produces only a score, and the engine can only declare winners or a draw. A cooperative game needs a win threshold.

changes.what: At the start of each turn, the engine sends the active player, through a private channel, the faces of every other player's hand plus only the IDs of their own hand.
changes.why: This states the supported mechanism for owner-blind hands. Only the active player needs the view, so one step per turn is enough.
changes.fixes: Owner-blind hands are the inverse of supported hidden hands, and the mechanism for showing each player the other hands was not stated.

changes.what: Remove the copies-outstanding table entirely. Players work it out themselves from the public discard pile and the three pile values, both shown every turn.
changes.why: This removes 15 attributes and all the lookup updates. The information is still fully available, and doing the counting is part of the reasoning.
changes.fixes: The previous variation tracked a copies-outstanding table of 15 numbers. That pushed the tracked numbers to at least 23, over the limit of 20.

changes.what: No colour-by-rank cell is ever updated. Cards are strings such as 'R3' in game lists (deck, hands, discard pile), and only the three pile values change.
changes.why: Without a table there is nothing to look up, so plays and discards cost a few list operations.
changes.fixes: Updating a 15-cell colour-by-rank table on every play or discard needs lookup logic the engine lacks, costing roughly 15 to 20 steps by itself.

changes.what: Keep only: piles R, G and B; hint tokens; fuses; deck count; turns played; final-round counter; team score; target; the action this turn; a play-success flag; the deck, discard and hint-log lists; and each player's hand list and score. That is 17 in all.
changes.why: This is an honest attribute budget under 20.
changes.fixes: The copies table is redundant. It can be derived exactly from the public discard pile and pile values, so it spends budget without adding information.

changes.what: Recount the turn as 18 explicit steps, each with a `when` condition. The 4 ordered end checks are merged into 2 steps that use `or`. The final round is handled by one counter, decremented before it is triggered.
changes.why: This gives an honest step count within the 20-step limit, with every rule accounted for.
changes.fixes: The previous step count (12) was understated. Validation, hint resolution, the play test, the pile update, fuses, bonuses, the draw, the final round and the end checks were not all counted.

changes.what: Resolve the validity check, hint matching and the play test each as a single referee rule check. Examples: 'list the IDs in the named hand whose card has the named colour or rank'; 'the revealed card's rank equals its colour's pile value plus 1'. The pile is then raised by one step with three `if` operations.
changes.why: Each of these replaces several per-card or per-colour comparison steps with one step.
changes.fixes: Hint matching done card by card, and the play test done as a 3-way colour lookup, would each cost several steps per turn.

keeps: Fully cooperative play: one shared outcome for the whole team.
Owner-blind hands: you see everyone's cards but your own.
The three actions (hint, discard, play) and the economy of 8 hint tokens and 3 fuses.
Hints must point to all matching cards of one colour or one rank, and so give negative information about the other cards.
Discarding regains a hint token; completing a pile to 5 regains one.
The deck mix of three 1s, two each of 2 to 4, and a single 5 per colour, so 5s must be protected.
The final round after the deck empties, and losing everything on the last fuse.
No table talk: all communication goes through hints.

recommendation.reason: Hanabi is a strong reasoning game: hidden information, inference from hints, and modelling a partner's intent. Cut down to 3 colours with a team target, and with the derivable copies table removed, it fits the limits.

variation.name: Hanabi: Three Fireworks
variation.summary: A cooperative 2 to 4 player Hanabi with a 30-card deck in 3 colours. Players see every hand but their own and communicate only through limited hints. The team must build fireworks worth a target score before the deck runs out or the third fuse burns.
variation.objective: When the game ends, every player's total equals the team score: the sum of the three pile tops, or 0 if the last fuse was lost. If that total is at least the target (10 with 2 or 3 players, 9 with 4 players), every player wins together. Otherwise no player reaches the target, the team has lost, and the engine records the result as no winner (a shared draw). No player can ever win alone.
variation.expected_effect: Play stays as hard as Hanabi on a smaller scale. Players must read hints for intent ('why did they point at that card now?'), count unseen copies themselves from the discard pile, protect the three singleton 5s, and time discards against the hint economy. Simple policies lose: blind playing burns 3 fuses and ends at 0, always discarding or always hinting builds nothing, and random play fails. The target of 10 out of 15 (9 with 4 players, who get smaller hands and a shorter deck) leaves slack for an unlucky shuffle, so the deal limits the ceiling but does not decide the result. Talk is deliberately left out: every player wants the same outcome, so there is nothing to disagree about, and free talk would let players simply state each other's cards and destroy the hint economy that is the game. Endgame unraveling does not apply, because the game is fully cooperative and judged against a target.

balanced.evidence:
This is a fully cooperative game with one shared outcome. Every total equals the team score, and the team wins with at least 1 fuse left and score at least 10 (2-3 players) or at least 9 (4 players). There is no opponent, so payoff ordering, dominance between players and seat edge do not arise. Every seat is on the same side, the turn order is fixed and public, and each player has the same information pattern: they see every hand except their own.

The real question is whether a thoughtless policy wins. Applying the WINNER RULE to each policy, played by all seats or mixed with a sensible partner:

| Policy | What happens | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Always discard the first card | Pile total stays 0. With 2 players the deck runs out after 20 discards, plus 2 final turns. | LOSE (0 < 10) |
| Always play the first card | Turn-1 success chance is 9/30 = 30%. Later the chance that a blind card is exactly the next rank is about 15-25%. Three failures come within about 4-6 plays. | LOSE (fuses reach 0) |
| Always the first option (HINT Red to the next seat) | 8 hints are spent. After that each hint is invalid (0 tokens or no Red) and becomes discard-oldest. No card is ever played. | LOSE (0) |
| Always the last option (PLAY your last card) | Same as blind play. | LOSE (fuses) |
| Uniformly random action | About 1/3 of actions are blind plays at roughly 20% success, so fuses run out before about 3 successes. | LOSE in almost every game |
| Sensible hint-driven play | Can reach 10/15. | WIN in most deals |

No action is safe in all states. Blind play burns fuses, endless discarding never scores, and hinting alone never scores.

Feasibility of the target, 2 players: 20 deck cards plus 2 final turns gives 22 card actions. 10 must be plays, leaving up to 12 discards. Hints available are 8 + 12 + completions, about 20. The turn budget is 22 card actions + 18 hints = 40, within the cap.

Feasibility, 4 players: 14 deck cards plus 4 final turns gives 18 card actions, since 12 cards stay stranded in hands. 9 must be plays, leaving up to 9 discards and at most 17 hints. That fits the 40 turns.

No 5 is needed for either target: 4+3+3 = 10, and 3+3+3 = 9. So the target is reachable but not trivial, and only coordinated play achieves it.

playable.evidence:
Rules completeness is good. Hint, discard, play, draw, invalid-action replacement, the final round and the end-check order are all specified. The game is finite: at most 40 turns, ending earlier on deck-out, 3 fuses, or a score of 15. The result is arithmetic on kept numbers. Leaving out talk is correct: everyone wants the same outcome, and talk would destroy the hint economy. Hints are sequential, which is the point of the game. The betrayal check does not apply because the game is cooperative.

The stated complexity, however, is understated and breaks the limits.

(1) Attributes. The copies-outstanding table alone is 3 colours x 5 ranks = 15 numbers. Add:
- 3 pile values
- hint tokens
- fuses
- deck count
- turn number
- target

That is 23 tracked numbers, over the limit of 20. This also ignores hand lists, deck list, discard list and hint log. The designer's figure of 15 cannot include all of these.

(2) Steps per round. The engine has no lookup operation. Every discard and every play must decrement exactly one of 15 table cells chosen by colour and rank. By the platform's own figure (about 13 steps for a 9-cell matrix), a 15-cell update costs roughly 15-20 steps. Each turn then also needs:
- the action choice
- validation (hint with 0 tokens, no match, self-target, card not in hand)
- hint resolution across a hand of up to 5 cards
- the play check against the pile of the card's colour (a 3-way conditional)
- the pile update
- fuse loss
- the completion bonus
- the discard token gain, capped at 8
- the draw
- the score calculation
- 4 ordered end checks

This is well over 20 steps, not the stated 12.

The table is also redundant. It is fully derivable from the public discard pile and pile values, so it costs budget without adding information.

(3) Visibility. Hands are hidden from their owner but visible to others, which is the inverse of the supported hidden_hands. It needs a per-player private_channel view of the other hands every turn. That is workable, but it should be stated as the mechanism.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
Chance enters only through the single opening shuffle. After that, the outcome depends on inference: deducing your own unseen cards from the hint log, the discard pile and the visible hands, and reading what a teammate's hint implies about which card is safe to play. It also depends on planning: hint-token economy, choosing which card to discard, and protecting the last copy of a card. There is plenty to infer and a direct way to act on it, by playing, discarding or hinting.

Under good play, the deal does not decide the result alone. The target needs no 5s, and every rank 2-4 has 2 copies, so a single bad discard is recoverable. Bad deals do exist, for example both copies of a needed 2 stuck in hands at deck-out in 4-player games where 12 cards are stranded, or critical cards drawn late. These cost perhaps 10-25% of games for strong teams.

The three tested policies sit at a 0% win rate (see balanced), while competent hint-driven play wins most deals. That gap is driven by reasoning, not luck. My estimate of chance's share of the outcome among competent teams is about 20-30%.

One caveat that is not a failure: because the outcome is shared, a strong model paired with a weak one gets the same score. Individual credit is therefore not separable, and the platform should evaluate team compositions rather than seats.

required_changes: Remove the copies-outstanding table from the state. It is derivable from the public discard pile plus pile values, and keeping it adds 15 attributes and about 15-20 lookup steps per turn. If a summary is wanted, have the engine print it as derived text, not as tracked attributes.

Recount the complexity honestly and keep tracked numbers to 20 or fewer: 3 piles, hints, fuses, deck count, turn, and the target as a constant. Store cards as a game list of strings such as 'R3', not as per-card attributes, and keep hands, deck, discard pile and hint log as lists.

Bring the turn to 20 steps or fewer by resolving the play test as one referee rule check ('the named card's rank equals its colour's pile value + 1'). Follow it with one step whose three `if` operations raise the matching pile, then single steps for fuse loss, completion bonus, discard token gain (capped at 8), draw, score calc, and two or three end checks.
Resolve hint matching as one referee/list step that returns the matching IDs in the target hand, rather than one comparison step per card.
State explicitly that each player's view of the other hands' faces is delivered through the private_channel every turn, because owner-blind hands are the inverse of the supported hidden_hands.

balanced.evidence:
This is a fully cooperative game. Every player's total is set to the same team score, and all win or all draw together. Seat order therefore gives no player an edge over another. Information is symmetric: each player sees every hand except their own.

Card counts check out:
- 3 colours x (3+2+2+2+1) = 30 cards.
- 2 players: 2x5 = 10 dealt, 20 in deck.
- 3 players: 3x4 = 12 dealt, 18 in deck.
- 4 players: 4x4 = 16 dealt, 14 in deck.

Target feasibility: the maximum is 15. Losing a single 5 caps a colour at 4, so the maximum becomes 14. A target of 10 (or 9 with 4 players) leaves slack but cannot be reached by luck.

Winner rule applied to thoughtless policies (2 players):

| Policy | What happens | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Always PLAY oldest | Only 9/30 = 30% of cards (the 1s) are playable at the start, and later plays need exact successors. About 3 failures come within the first 4-6 plays, fuses hit 0 and the score is forced to 0. | Loss against every teammate behaviour that does not stop it |
| Always DISCARD oldest | Piles stay at 0. The deck runs out after 20 discards plus 2 final turns, score 0. | Loss |
| Always HINT (first option) | 8 legal hints. At 0 tokens a hint is invalid and becomes discard oldest (+1 token), then hint, then discard, and so on. No play ever happens, score 0. | Loss |
| 'Always the highest' / last option (PLAY) | Same as always PLAY. | Loss |
| Uniform random legal action | About 1/3 of actions are blind plays. Expected blind plays before 3 failures is about 4-5, and that blind-play rate burns 3 fuses well before the deck runs out, so the result is almost always score 0. | Loss |

No thoughtless policy wins or even avoids the loss. No action is strictly dominant: playing, hinting and discarding each matter depending on state.

Payoff labelling: the team score is the sum of pile tops, 0 on 3 fuses. The described win condition is 'score >= target'. The numbers match the description.
balanced.evidence_note: The 'higher total wins' failure mode does not apply: there is no competitive comparison and all totals are identical.

playable.evidence:
Rules are complete. Each of the three actions has explicit legality conditions, and every invalid case is enumerated with a defined default (DISCARD oldest). Token cap (8), fuse loss, pile-completion bonus, draw timing, and the ID system (stable public IDs, faces hidden from the owner) are all specified. Play on a completed pile simply fails by the 'exactly 1 more' rule.

Final-round arithmetic:
- The counter is set to N on the drawing turn and is not decremented that turn.
- Each later turn decrements it. After N more turns it reaches 0, so each player, the drawer last, gets exactly one more turn.
- Hands never empty: with 2 players a 5-card hand loses at most 1 card in the final round.

Finiteness:
- Turns before the deck empties = draws + hints, where hints <= 8 + discards + completed piles.
- 4 players: at most about 14 + (8+14) + 4 = 40.
- 2 players: about 20 + 20 + 2 = 42 is possible (10 plays, 10 discards, heavy hinting). The 40-turn cap could then truncate the final round. This is explicitly stated and announced via 'turns played', so it is a known planning constraint, not an ambiguity.
- The game always terminates.

Scoring is pure arithmetic on tracked numbers. No judge is needed for the outcome; legality and hint matching are simple membership and equality checks.

Complexity against limits:
- steps 18 <= 20;
- choice steps 1 <= 4;
- attributes 17 <= 20;
- hidden elements 2 <= 3 (own hand faces, deck order);
- random draws 0 <= 1 (the single shuffle is setup, and draws come from the shuffled list via remove/append);
- rounds 40 <= 40.

The 18-step count is tight but plausible, since conditional `if` operations per step cover the play/discard/hint branches. Inverse visibility (everyone but the owner) is done through the supported private_channel. The deck uses the shared_deck_draw workaround. There is no board, clock, trading or binding agreement.

Talk: correctly omitted. Players want the same outcome, and free talk would let teammates simply read out each other's hands, removing the entire inference problem. Constrained communication via hints is the designed channel, so players are not reduced to blind guessing. Turns are inherently sequential (one active player), so sequential choice is correct here.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
Chance is the single initial shuffle. Everything after it is decided by inference and planning:
- **Hint economy:** 8 tokens shared by a team that must make 10+ successful plays.
- **Implicature:** inferring why a teammate gave a particular hint, or chose to discard rather than hint.
- **Card counting:** using the discard pile and piles to know which cards are last copies (all 5s, and the second copy of 2-4).
- **Risk management:** fuses.

Under intended good play (systematic hint conventions inferred from the log, protecting critical cards, discarding known-safe cards) a 3-colour, 30-card deck with 8 tokens should typically reach 12-15. The target of 10 (9 with 4 players) leaves room to lose most of one colour. Only rare deals defeat good play, for example a 5 and both copies of its 4 clustered at the bottom of the deck past the final round. Estimated share of outcomes decided by the shuffle when both teams play well: roughly 10-15%. Thoughtless or random play scores 0 almost always (see balanced).

There is plenty to infer, and the action set lets players act on it:
- your own hand, from hints and from what teammates do and do not hint;
- teammates' knowledge state, from the public log;
- remaining copies.

Caveat: because the result is shared, a strong reasoner paired with a weak one gets the same outcome. Reasoning is rewarded at the team level across games, which is the standard Hanabi benchmark property, not a chance problem.
